title: COVID-19 Vaccine Information and Infertility Posts on X: Insights on a Misinformation Pandemic
screen_reason: Retrospective content analysis of English-language X (Twitter) posts about COVID-19 vaccination and fertility, drawn from the COVID-19-TweetIDs dataset across two event windows in 2021 and hand-screened by the study team as factual or misinformation. It reports the share of items in a sample classified as misinformation with an explicit denominator - 3,422/11,436 (29.9%) in timeframe 1 and 2,699/5,982 (45.1%) in timeframe 2 - which is a CONTENT estimate.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language posts with no geographic filter, compared against daily average US COVID-19 case counts
estimates.date: Timeframe 1: 16 July 2021 - 13 August 2021 (representative point chosen; timeframe 2 was 5 November - 3 December 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of relevant English-language X posts about COVID-19 vaccination and fertility that were classified as misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 3422 (29.9%) of 11,436 relevant posts in timeframe 1; the paper's other window gives 2699 (45.1%) of 5,982 relevant posts in timeframe 2
estimates.denominator: 11,436 original English-language X posts judged relevant to COVID-19 vaccination and fertility/pregnancy/conception, screened from the 16,547 posts (0.1%) that matched the keyword lists within 17,884,132 English original posts in timeframe 1
estimates.definition: A post was counted as misinformation if it stated factually incorrect information, judged by a trained screener who assessed the content for validity, opened all embedded links and weighed the poster's tone and intent; a post repeating a false claim while flagging or mocking it as false was classified as FACTUAL, so the numerator is endorsed falsehood, not mere mention
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation was defined as posts stating factually incorrect information."
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation posts rose from 29.9% in July 2021 to 45.1%
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'X posts analyzed', p. 50, with Figure 1 (study flow); restated in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Screened by study team members (medical students and physicians) who were 'trained on post inclusion criteria before data collection'; screeners opened embedded links and assessed validity and tone, and 'all posts ambiguous in categorization were discussed among the group, and a consensus was reached'. No inter-rater reliability coefficient, no double-coded subsample and no count of posts sent to adjudication are reported, and the number of screeners is not stated - the weakest link in an otherwise well-specified pipeline.
estimates.moderator_quote: posts had to contain one word from a list of terms related to COVID-19 vaccination (Pfizer, Moderna, J&J, Johnson and Johnson, vaccine, vax, antivax, NoCovidVax, mRNA, warp speed, vaxxed, Covidiots, Sheeple, herd immunity) and one word from a list of terms related to fertility (infertility, fertility, IVF, egg freezing, Ivfwarrior, TTC, IUI, infertile, embryo, womenshealth, pregnant, placenta, abortion, miscarriage, pregnancy, obstetric, birth defect, fetus, eggs).
estimates.notes: COLLAPSE DECISION, stated explicitly as the protocol requires. The paper reports the same measure in two purposively chosen, non-overlapping event windows: 29.9% (3,422/11,436) around the ACOG/SMFM pregnancy-safety guidance of 30 July 2021, and 45.1% (2,699/5,982) around the CDC booster announcement of 19 November 2021. Following the rule to collapse to one representative point, I have taken TIMEFRAME 1, because it carries the larger relevant-post denominator (11,436 of the 17,418 total, 66%). I did NOT pool the two windows: 6,121/17,418 = 35.1% would be a cross-category sum I computed, which R8 forbids. If the review's convention is instead to keep both event windows as separate rows, the second row is fully specified here and in missed_or_uncertain and can be added without re-reading the paper - the choice moves this study's estimate between 29.9% and 45.1%, so it is not cosmetic. Note the denominator is only the keyword-matched, relevance-screened 0.1% of English COVID-19 posts, i.e. a narrow single-issue corpus (COVID vaccine AND fertility), not a general measure of misinformation on X; the authors deliberately excluded adjacent claims (aborted-fetal-cell content, male fertility), which narrows it further. Restricted to original posts - reposts were removed - so this is production, not circulation. The article text is two-column with hyphenated line breaks, so the Results sentence carrying the counts is not quotable as a contiguous span; the source_quote is the abstract's statement of the same figure and the full counts are in rob.item10_quote.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) Timeframe 2's 2699 (45.1%) of 5,982 - held out only because of the collapse rule, not on quality grounds; it is equally verbatim ("From the relevant posts from timeframe 2, 3283 (54.9%) were deemed factual and 2699 (45.1%) were deemed misinformation") and if the review keeps event windows separately this is the row to add: same country/platform/definition/ground truth, date 5 November - 3 December 2021, denominator 5,982 relevant posts screened from 11,474 keyword-flagged posts within 11,559,569 English originals. (2) The pooled 17,418 posts / 35.1% - never printed by the authors; it would be my own cross-category sum, barred by R8. (3) The verified-user shares (factual 1607/8014 = 20.1% vs misinformation 58/3422 = 1.7% in timeframe 1; 569/3283 = 17.3% vs 20/2699 = 0.7% in timeframe 2). These are the share of posts WITHIN each veracity class coming from verified accounts, i.e. a source composition of an already-classified set, not a prevalence share and not a concentration statistic (no top-X% of accounts is mapped to a share of activity, so R1's requirement for both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct cannot be met). (4) Sentiment distributions (misinformation 50.9% negative / 12.1% neutral / 37.0% positive in timeframe 1) and mean compound sentiment scores - tone, not veracity, and computed within the misinformation class. (5) Engagement means (followers 86,034.2 vs 3,969.9; reposts 4.9 vs 4.5; favorites 21.6 vs 14.2; posts per user 1.3 vs 1.2) - means, not shares, and again within-class. These are the closest thing to an exposure or amplification measure in the paper, but no share of impressions, views or reshares attributable to misinformation is reported, so no SHARING or EXPOSURE row is possible. (6) '0.1%' of all English COVID-19 posts matched the keyword lists (16,547/17,884,132 and 11,474/11,559,569) - a keyword-yield rate, not a misinformation share; note the 69.1% and 52.1% relevance rates are shares of the flagged sets, also not veracity. (7) Correlations between misinformation rate and daily US COVID-19 cases, and the within-window trends (-0.49 in timeframe 1, +0.39 in timeframe 2, which run in opposite directions) - these are the actual time series, correctly collapsed away. (8) '29.3% of verified physician accounts are women' - cited from reference 19, barred by R8. Minor inconsistency: the abstract labels timeframe 2 as both 'November 2021' and 'December 2021'; the Methods date range 5 Nov - 3 Dec 2021 is authoritative.

rob.design: Retrospective observational content analysis. Source: the public COVID-19-TweetIDs repository, rehydrated through X's API, for two 4-week windows bracketing named events (ACOG/SMFM pregnancy guidance 30 July 2021; CDC booster announcement 19 November 2021). About 90 million posts per window were extracted, roughly 10% already deleted; restricted to English (per X's own language tag) and to original posts (reposts removed), leaving 17,884,132 and 11,559,569; keyword-filtered on the intersection of a COVID-vaccine term list and a fertility term list, yielding 16,547 and 11,474 (0.1% each); hand-screened for relevance to 11,436 (69.1%) and 5,982 (52.1%); each relevant post then classified factual or misinformation. Coding by trained study-team members with group consensus on ambiguous cases, but NO reported inter-rater reliability, no stated number of coders and no double-coding audit. Sentiment scored automatically (VADER-style compound score). Analysis in Python 3.9.1 and R 4.1.3; ANOVA and chi-square for group comparisons; deemed non-human-subjects research by the University of Miami IRB. Author-acknowledged limitations: keyword sampling bias (relevant posts may have been screened out), only two snapshots of a multi-year phenomenon, and no poster demographics. Further unacknowledged constraints for this review's purposes: English-only with no geographic attribution, deleted posts silently missing (~10%), and a denominator confined to one narrow topical intersection.
rob.item6_quote: Once determined to be relevant, the screener categorized the post as "factual" or "misinformation." Misinformation was defined as posts stating factually incorrect information. Screeners evaluated the content of the posts for validity, opened all embedded links, and assessed the post's tone. The intent of the poster was a key consideration. If a post stated false information and the recognition that the information was false (or, often, insulting the person who made the original claim), that message was classified as factual.
rob.item10_quote: From the pertinent posts of timeframe 1, 8014 (70.1%) were deemed factual and 3422 (29.9%) were deemed misinformation. For timeframe 2, 11,474 (0.1%) were flagged with the selected keywords and screened for relevancy, with 5982 (52.1%) posts marked as relevant. From the relevant posts from timeframe 2, 3283 (54.9%) were deemed factual and 2699 (45.1%) were deemed misinformation.
